> 不尚贤，使民不争.

This line has a reputation. It is read as the oldest manual for keeping people docile: don't honor talent, don't prize rare goods, keep them fed and ignorant. Plato's noble lie, one chapter earlier.

The reading is wrong, and it is wrong in a specific way: it takes the object of the three 不 to be people, when the object is a scale.

## Three ways of raising something

尚 is to lift something up onto a platform. 貴 is to put a price on it. 見 — read xiàn here, "to display," not "to see" — is to place it where it catches the eye.

Three characters, three ways of elevating. Three 不, one action: do not raise the standard yourself.

賢 is a capacity a person actually has. 難得之貨 is an object that actually exists. Neither carries rank or price on its own; rank and price are added by people. Once you praise it, price it, and put it on display, you have handed everyone a ruler to measure each other with. The ruler appears, comparison starts; comparison starts, contention and theft follow; contention and theft start, and the ground of the heart is churned up.

So the chapter does not deny 賢, does not deny goods, does not deny desire. It denies the ruler.

## Why 尚賢 was a live problem, not a slogan

At the end of the Spring and Autumn period, 尚賢 was progressive politics.

Mozi argued that office should not follow blood: 官無常貴，民無終賤 — promote the capable, demote the incapable. That was a blade against hereditary privilege, opening a path for 士 to rise on ability. Confucius, asked about government, answered 舉賢才: raise the straight and place them over the crooked, and the crooked will straighten.

The problem is what happens when 賢 becomes a slot. A standard for selection is also a position to be competed for. By the late Spring and Autumn, 士 were traveling between states seeking office, salary, and a name. Recommendation power sat with ministers; the recommended owed gratitude, the recommender collected reputation. The selection of the worthy quickly entangled with private favor and public vanity.

不尚賢，使民不爭 is not an argument against capable people holding office. It is an observation: as long as 賢 is a quota that others evaluate and others compete for, contention is unavoidable — and what is being contested is not the work, it is the title.

## The four things a ruler is supposed to do instead

> 虛其心，實其腹；弱其志，強其骨.

Four operations, two pairs, and they map onto the cup from chapter 1.

- 實其腹 and 強其骨 thicken and firm the wall. Feed what life actually requires; establish the boundary a person stands on. A vessel with no wall holds nothing.
- 虛其心 and 弱其志 open the hollow. Clear comparison, calculation, and the chase after external marks; loosen the ambition that exists only by comparing with someone else.

Note what 弱其志 does not say. It does not say "remove ambition." 志 is where you are going; the 妄志 being weakened is the need to be ahead of someone. Direction stays. The comparison goes.

The reading example is almost too ordinary: learn the material properly, that is 實腹強骨; stop staking everything on the ranking, that is 虛心弱志. Ranking is wall, not use. A person watching the wall never gets quiet enough to digest anything, because the ruler has filled the hollow.

## 無知無欲 is not stupidity

> 常使民無知無欲，使夫智者不敢為也.

This is the most misread line in the book, and it needs to be read on two levels.

Grammatically, 知 here is 分別之知 — the faculty that ranks, compares, and calculates advantage; 欲 is 攀緣之欲 — wanting that hangs on an external mark. What is being stilled is that operation, not cognition as such. 實其腹 already left ordinary need in place. The chapter did not ask anyone to stop eating.

Experientially, the line points to 知無 — seeing that the hollow is what does the work. A vessel's use is not the wall but the space the wall encloses. A person's steadiness is not the mark but the cleared place inside.

So the line is neither "keep them stupid" nor "want nothing." What it removes is the machinery of measuring people and measuring yourself. Capacity to learn, judge, and improve is untouched.

## The trap: grasping at emptiness

There is a failure mode that catches almost everyone who reads this chapter sympathetically.

You make 無 into a new target. You want to be empty, want to be desireless, and the wanting is itself 攀緣之欲; the emptiness you are chasing becomes a new 執取之有 — a stone you can hold.

Outward grabbing at money and name is grasping; inward grabbing at emptiness is also grasping. The first thickens the wall. The second turns the hollow into an object.

Which is why the chapter ends where it does: 為無為，則無不治. Not "do nothing and everything will be governed," but act in the mode of 無 — initiate, draw the boundary, build the carrier, and leave the position unlocked. The same instruction as chapter 1, now applied to governing and to studying and to the inside of one's own head.

## A test

Name one ranking you checked this week that you did not need in order to do the work. Then notice how much of your attention it took.
